Algebra I · Lesson 1.2

Order of Operations

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

An expression is only useful if every reader gets the same value from it. But some expressions can be read in more than one reasonable way, and different readings give different numbers. Before doing any algebra, we have to settle how expressions are read.

Problem
Two students evaluate 100−10×9100−10×9. The first works strictly left to right, subtracting before multiplying. The second does the multiplication first, then subtracts. Neither makes a single arithmetic slip, yet they land on different numbers. How far apart are their two answers?
Show a hint
  • Work each reading all the way to the end before comparing.
  • Left to right means (100−10)×9(100−10)×9. Multiplying first means 100−(10×9)100−(10×9).
Show the full solution
Reading left to right, 100−10=90100−10=90, then 90×9=81090×9=810. Multiplying first, 10×9=9010×9=90, then 100−90=10100−90=10. Two reasonable readings give 810810 and 1010, and the gap between them is 810−10=800810−10=800​.

Neither student made an arithmetic mistake, so checking the arithmetic cannot settle this. We need a rule that says which operation comes first, and mathematicians agreed on one long ago. From here on we also write multiplication as 3⋅93⋅9 or with parentheses, because algebra uses the letter x constantly and ×× is too easy to confuse with it.

Key idea
The order of operations. Grouping symbols go first, worked from the inside out when they nest. Then exponents. Then multiplication and division together, left to right. Then addition and subtraction together, left to right. The ranking is not arbitrary. An exponent is repeated multiplication and a product is repeated addition, so ranking each operation above the one it repeats means most expressions need no parentheses. Under this rule 100−10⋅9100−10⋅9 means multiply first. Its value is 1010, so the second student is right.
Problem
All four levels of the order show up in this one expression. Evaluate 5+(18−6)÷225+(18−6)÷22 doing the steps in the order the rule lists them.
Show a hint
  • Resolve 18−618−6 and 2222 before any dividing happens.
Show the full solution
Parentheses first, 18−6=1218−6=12. Exponent next, 22=422=4. Then the division, 12÷4=312÷4=3, and finally the addition, 5+3=85+3=8​.
Key idea
Equal rank, left to right. The list has four levels, not six. Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. Dividing by 44 is multiplying by 1441​. So division and multiplication are the same kind of operation, and neither outranks the other. Subtraction is addition of the opposite in the same way. When operations share a level, do them left to right. This is where PEMDAS misleads people, because the acronym lists multiplication ahead of division as if it came first.
Problem
Another disagreement. In 48÷6⋅248÷6⋅2, one student divides first and gets 8⋅2=168⋅2=16. The other multiplies 6⋅26⋅2 first and gets 48÷12=448÷12=4. Only one of them is right. Which value is correct?
Show a hint
  • Division and multiplication have equal rank, so rank cannot break the tie.
  • When rank ties, reading order decides.
Show the full solution
48÷6=848÷6=8, then 8⋅2=168⋅2=16​. The first student is right, because division and multiplication have equal rank and a tie is broken left to right, not in favor of multiplication.
Problem
One multiplication, one subtraction, one addition. Evaluate 19−8+2⋅319−8+2⋅3 keeping careful track of which of the three moves first, which second, and which last.
Show a hint
  • Only the multiplication outranks the rest, so it goes first.
  • Then subtraction and addition have equal rank. Read left to right.
Show the full solution
The multiplication goes first, 2⋅3=62⋅3=6, leaving 19−8+619−8+6. Subtraction and addition have equal rank, so work left to right, 19−8=1119−8=11, then 11+6=1711+6=17​. Doing the 8+68+6 first would give 19−14=519−14=5, which answers a different expression.
Key idea
Exponents come first after grouping. An exponent applies only to the one symbol it is attached to. A minus sign in front is not part of the base. It is a separate operation applied afterward. So −b2−b2 means the opposite of b2b2. Square first, then negate. (−b)2(−b)2 squares the negative number itself. Parentheses are the only way to include the sign in the base, so write (−b)2(−b)2 when you want that and read −b2−b2 as −(b2)−(b2) otherwise.
Problem
In 200−3⋅42200−3⋅42 the 44 sits between a multiplication and an exponent. Decide which one applies to it first, then evaluate.
Show a hint
  • The exponent applies only to the 44, not to 3⋅43⋅4.
Show the full solution
42=1642=16, then 3⋅16=483⋅16=48, and 200−48=152200−48=152​. The exponent applies only to the 44. Squaring 3⋅43⋅4 instead would give 200−144=56200−144=56.
Problem
Evaluate (−7)2+(−72)(−7)2+(−72). The two pieces look identical, so compute each one separately before adding.
Show a hint
  • The parentheses in (−7)2(−7)2 put the minus sign inside the base.
  • In −72−72 the exponent applies only to the 77. Square first, then negate.
Show the full solution
The first piece squares the negative itself, (−7)2=(−7)(−7)=49(−7)2=(−7)(−7)=49. The second squares first and negates after, −72=−(72)=−49−72=−(72)=−49. The sum is 49+(−49)=049+(−49)=0​.
Key idea
Fraction bars and radical bars group. A fraction bar groups its entire numerator and its entire denominator, as if each had parentheses around it. A radical bar groups everything it covers. Neither is written with parentheses, so putting a fraction on a single line means adding the parentheses yourself. a+bcca+b​ becomes (a+b)÷c(a+b)÷c, never a+b÷ca+b÷c.
Problem
Not one parenthesis appears in 22+2⋅1452−1552−1522+2⋅14​ yet two invisible pairs of them are at work. Evaluate the expression.
Show a hint
  • The bar wraps the whole top and the whole bottom. Finish each completely before dividing.
  • In the denominator, the exponent goes before the subtraction.
Show the full solution
On top, 2⋅14=282⋅14=28 and 22+28=5022+28=50. On the bottom, 52=2552=25 and 25−15=1025−15=10. Divide last, 50÷10=550÷10=5​. The bar groups the whole top and the whole bottom, so each side has to finish before any dividing happens.
Problem
Both 625625 and 4949 are perfect squares, which makes a certain shortcut very tempting. Evaluate 625−49625−49​ and resist it.
Show a hint
  • The radical bar groups everything under it. Subtract before any root is taken.
Show the full solution
The radical bar groups everything under it, so 625−49=576625−49=576 comes first, and 576=24576​=24​. Taking each root separately gives 25−7=1825−7=18, which answers a different expression.

When groups nest, work from the innermost group outward, passing each answer to the next layer. Square brackets mean exactly what parentheses mean and follow the same rules. They are easier to spot, which helps you keep the layers apart.

Problem
Two layers of grouping and one exponent. Evaluate 3[ 47−(11−5)2 ]3[47−(11−5)2] working from the innermost group outward.
Show a hint
  • Do the parentheses inside before the brackets outside.
  • Inside the brackets, the exponent still goes before the subtraction.
Show the full solution
Innermost first, 11−5=611−5=6. The exponent comes next, 62=3662=36, then inside the brackets 47−36=1147−36=11, and finally 3⋅11=333⋅11=33​.
Fun fact
The order of operations is an agreement, not a law of nature. A four-function calculator executes keystrokes as they arrive, so 3+4⋅203+4⋅20 comes back 140140. A scientific calculator reads the whole line first and answers 8383.
Problem
One expression carries every trap in the lesson, a tight exponent, a radical bar, and a fraction bar. Evaluate −34+11745−3645−36​−34+117​
Show a hint
  • The exponent applies only to the 33, so −34−34 means −(34)−(34).
  • Both bars group. Finish the whole top and the whole bottom before dividing.
Show the full solution
On top, −34=−(34)=−81−34=−(34)=−81, so the numerator is −81+117=36−81+117=36. On the bottom, the radical bar groups 45−36=945−36=9, and 9=39​=3. The fraction bar divides last, 36÷3=1236÷3=12​.

The whole rule is short. Groups first, worked inside out, then exponents, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. It only tells you how to read what is written. It does not tell you which changes to an expression are legal, which swaps and regroupings leave the value alone. That is the next lesson.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Start with a straight computation. Evaluate 46−5⋅3246−5⋅32, doing the operations in the order the rule assigns them.
Show the solution
The power goes first, 32=932=9, then the multiplication, 5⋅9=455⋅9=45, and last the subtraction, 46−45=146−45=1​.
Practice
In 60÷6⋅560÷6⋅5, a student multiplies 6⋅56⋅5 first because PEMDAS lists multiplication before division. Evaluate the expression correctly.
Show the solution
60÷6=1060÷6=10, then 10⋅5=5010⋅5=50​. Division and multiplication have equal rank, so the tie breaks left to right. Multiplying first would give 60÷30=260÷30=2, and PEMDAS listing M before D does not change that.
Practice
Evaluate 52−37+852−37+8. Subtraction and addition tie the same way division and multiplication do, and the same rule breaks the tie.
Show the solution
52−37=1552−37=15, then 15+8=2315+8=23​. Subtraction and addition have equal rank, so read left to right. Doing 37+837+8 first would give 52−45=752−45=7.
Practice
Evaluate −26−26. Before you compute anything, decide exactly what the exponent applies to and what the minus sign is doing.
Show the solution
The exponent applies only to the 22, so −26−26 means −(26)=−64−(26)=−64​. Only (−2)6(−2)6, with written parentheses, puts the whole −2−2 under the exponent, and that one comes out at positive 6464.
Practice
Evaluate 34−(−3)334−(−3)3. This time the parentheses are written in, so the exponent applies to the whole −3−3.
Show the solution
(−3)3=−27(−3)3=−27, then 34−(−27)=34+27=6134−(−27)=34+27=61​. The written parentheses put the whole −3−3 under the exponent, and an odd power keeps the negative sign.
Practice
Evaluate 75−32⋅42⋅475−3​. Written carelessly on a single line this expression would mean something different, so keep the bar's grouping in mind.
Show the solution
Finish the top and the bottom before dividing. The top is 75−3=7275−3=72 and the bottom is 2⋅4=82⋅4=8, so the value is 72÷8=972÷8=9​.
Practice
Evaluate 144+25144+25​. Both numbers under the bar happen to be perfect squares, which makes the wrong shortcut look extra inviting.
Show the solution
The bar covers the whole sum, so add first, 144+25=169144+25=169, and then 169=13169​=13​. Taking each root separately gives 12+5=1712+5=17, which answers a different expression.
Practice
Evaluate 84÷[2⋅(9−2)]84÷[2⋅(9−2)]. Two layers of grouping, so work from the inside out.
Show the solution
Inside out, 9−2=79−2=7, then 2⋅7=142⋅7=14, and finally 84÷14=684÷14=6​. Ignoring the brackets and reading straight through would give 84÷2⋅7=29484÷2⋅7=294.
Practice
Evaluate 9+54÷32⋅29+54÷32⋅2. One short line that uses every level below grouping, including a left-to-right tie.
Show the solution
The power goes first, 32=932=9. Division and multiplication tie, so work left to right, 54÷9=654÷9=6, then 6⋅2=126⋅2=12, and adding the 99 in front gives 2121​.
Practice
Parentheses outrank everything, so one well-placed pair can transform a value. Insert a single pair of parentheses into 2⋅6+322⋅6+32 to make the result as large as possible, then enter that largest value.
Show the solution
Wrapping everything before the exponent gives (2⋅6+3)2=152=225(2⋅6+3)2=152=225​. Every other placement is smaller, since 2⋅(6+3)2=1622⋅(6+3)2=162 and 2⋅(6+32)=302⋅(6+32)=30.
